answer:
**A feature store must answer two different questions.** Online serving asks, “What is the latest valid value for this user now?” Training asks, “What value would have been available when this historical prediction was made?” A database that answers the first question quickly does not automatically answer the second correctly.

**An example of subtle leakage.** A transaction occurred at 10:00 but arrived in the feature pipeline at 10:05. A model prediction made at 10:02 could not have used it, even though its event timestamp is earlier than the prediction. Training joins must respect availability time as well as event time when that distinction matters. [1](https://docs.feast.dev/getting-started/concepts/point-in-time-joins)

Store feature definitions, entity keys, versions, timestamps, and freshness requirements. Keep historical records for point-in-time reconstruction and materialize current values into a low-latency online store. Share transformation logic where possible, but test actual results: matching function names are not proof of matching behavior.

**Handle updates deliberately.** An older delayed event should not overwrite a newer current value without a defined recomputation policy. Retries should be idempotent. A model version must request compatible feature versions, and missing/stale values need explicit defaults or fallbacks.

Measure train–serve skew by replaying logged serving examples and comparing values, not by claiming an architecture guarantees zero skew. Monitor latency, missingness, freshness, and hot keys separately. A feature store is useful infrastructure, but it cannot repair a fundamentally leaky label definition or make unavailable future information legitimate training input.

**Technical details and references.**

Define each feature with entity keys, transformation version, event time, availability/ingestion time, and freshness requirements. Keep an immutable offline history and materialize the latest valid values into an online key-value store. For training, retrieve only data that would have been available at prediction time; event-time filtering alone can leak a late-arriving record that was not yet known.

Share transformation definitions between batch and streaming paths and validate them with replay/parity tests. Materialization should be idempotent and reject older updates that arrive after newer ones. Include feature versions in model dependencies, and deploy compatible model/feature revisions together. Online requests need bounded timeouts, freshness metadata, and defined defaults for absent values.

No architecture guarantees literally zero train-serve skew. Measure value discrepancies, missingness, lateness, and transformation drift; replay logged serving inputs to diagnose failures. Partition online keys by entity, monitor hot keys, and backfill offline history without silently rewriting serving state. The tradeoff is fast current lookups versus faithful historical reconstruction; one store rarely serves both workloads equally well.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A point-in-time join must respect both event time and when the information became available. Formally a training feature at prediction time t may use only records available by t under the production contract. Replay sampled online requests against offline reconstruction and measure discrepancy distributions, rather than assuming shared feature names imply identical values. [3](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://docs.feast.dev/getting-started/concepts/point-in-time-joins) and [2](https://huyenchip.com/2023/01/08/self-serve-feature-platforms.html).
